claims.text: HEAs can exhibit enhanced resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in harsh environments.
Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by rapid formation and adaptive self-healing of a multi-component passive film.
Increasing concentrations of oxide-forming elements such as Cr and Al enables rapid passive-film formation and self-healing.
The passive film limits exposure of fresh metal during wear and thereby reduces corrosion damage.
The initial as-cast or thermomechanically processed HEA exhibits native microstructural heterogeneities.
Increasing Cr and Al while maintaining a similar microstructure provides a controlled chemistry comparison.
Mechanical wear repeatedly disrupts the passive film.
The tailored alloy composition facilitates rapid reformation of a protective multi-component oxide layer after disruption.
Rapid oxide-layer reformation minimizes the duration or extent of fresh-metal exposure.
Minimizing fresh-metal exposure concurrently reduces wear depth and corrosion current under synergistic degradation conditions.
The Cr- and Al-enriched alloy will have lower wear depth than the matched baseline HEA during tribocorrosion.
The Cr- and Al-enriched alloy will have lower corrosion current density than the matched baseline HEA during tribocorrosion.
The predicted benefit holds under moderate mechanical and corrosive conditions that permit sufficient passive-film reformation time.
The benefit diminishes or fails when excessive wear intensity or electrolyte aggressiveness exceeds passive-film self-healing kinetics.
The mechanical-stress and electrolyte-aggressiveness thresholds for failure of passive-film self-healing are not quantified.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction exceeding about 20% in both wear depth and corrosion current density would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe a dynamically reforming multi-component passive film during testing would falsify the hypothesis.
